question: A 3-year-old presents with 2 weeks of fever, irritability, and neck stiffness. CSF analysis shows: WBC 180/mm³ (90% lymphocytes), protein 280 mg/dL, glucose 28 mg/dL (concurrent blood glucose 90 mg/dL), and xanthochromic appearance. Which type of meningitis does this CSF profile MOST strongly suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial meningitis typically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis (>80% neutrophils), very high protein, and very low glucose. A predominantly lymphocytic CSF with subacute onset makes bacterial meningitis much less likely.

Viral meningitis shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and mildly elevated protein, but the glucose is NORMAL (CSF:serum ratio >0.6). The very low CSF glucose (28/90 = 0.31 ratio) and high protein (280 mg/dL) make viral meningitis incorrect.

This profile is classic for TBM: subacute onset (weeks), lymphocytic pleocytosis, markedly elevated protein (>200 mg/dL), and low CSF glucose (CSF:serum ratio 28/90 = 0.31, i.e. <0.5). The glucose is the key differentiator from viral meningitis — TBM and bacterial meningitis both lower CSF glucose, but TBM has lymphocytes, not neutrophils.

Cryptococcal meningitis can produce a similar lymphocytic picture with low glucose. However, in a 3-year-old in India, TBM is far more common than cryptococcal meningitis (the latter occurs mainly in immunocompromised hosts). Ink preparation for cryptococcal capsules would distinguish them.

overallFeedback.feedback: Apply the five-step CSF interpretation framework: (1) cell type — lymphocytes; (2) protein — very high; (3) glucose — very low (ratio 0.31); (4) tempo — subacute weeks; (5) other features — high protein xanthochromia. Low glucose + lymphocytes = TBM or fungal, not viral. TBM is the correct answer in this clinical context.

Correct. The combination of subacute onset (weeks), lymphocytic pleocytosis, very high protein, and very low glucose (ratio <0.5) is the hallmark CSF profile for TBM. Glucose <0.5 of blood glucose with lymphocytic cells distinguishes TBM from viral meningitis (normal glucose) and from bacterial meningitis (neutrophilic cells).
